notes.2i: Some candidates used tan 45 = (vertical velocity)/(horizontal velocity) instead of tan 45 = (vertical distance)/(horizontal distance).
notes.2iii: This part of the question was generally well done with many candidates obtaining full marks. Answers: (i) v = 8.2(0) ms–1; (ii) t = 0.3(00) s.
notes.3: Many candidates scored all marks on this question.
notes.3i: By using T = λx/L many candidates went on to score both the available marks.
notes.3iii: If d is the greatest distance then 20(d – 0.4)2/(2 x 0.4) = 0.25gd. This sets up a quadratic equation and when solved results in the greatest distance. Answers: (i) Distance OP = 0.45 m; (ii) Speed = 2.92 ms–1; (iii) Greatest distance OP = 0.656 m.
notes.4i: This part of the question was solved by using tan θ = 0.7/(2.4/4), θ = 49.4°.
notes.4iii: This part is solved by setting up an equation by taking moments about some point. If moments are taken about the vertex V then the equation becomes 4w x VG =w x 2.4 x 3 + 3 w (2.4 + h/2) with G as the centre of mass of the whole solid. If α is the semi-vertical angle of the cone then tan α = 0.7/2.4 and so cos α = 2.4/2.5. VG = 2.5/cos α = 2.5/(2.4/2.5) = 125/48 and so 4 x 125/48 = 0.6 x 3 + 7.2 +1.5h giving h = 0.994 m. Answers: (i) θ = 49.4°; (ii) Greatest possible value of h = 1.2 m; (iii) Least possible value of h = 0.994 m
notes.5: This question was a good source of marks for many candidates.
notes.5i: Few candidates did not set up the given equation. Most candidates integrated correctly to set up a logarithmic function. A number of candidates did not manipulate the algebra to get the correct function for v in terms of t.
notes.5iii: Full marks were often scored on this part of the question. Those candidates who had mistaken expressions v could often still obtain marks. Answers: (i) v = 50 – 50e −0.2t;
notes.6: This question caused problems. Few candidates gained full marks.
notes.6i: Many candidates did not realise that the length of AB was 0.7 m and not 0.9 m. If θ is the angle that AB makes with the vertical then sin θ = 0.2/0.7. By resolving vertically the tension can now be found. Having found the tension then by using radial acceleration the value of ω can be calculated. It is then possible to find the kinetic energy.
notes.6iii: Here it is necessary to first find the distance AB. This can be done by using the right angled triangle ABC with BC = 0.9 – AB and then stating that tan BAC = (0.9 – AB)/AB =1/2. This gives AB = 0.6. The radius of the circle is then equal to 0.6 sin BAC. T can now be calculated by resolving vertically giving T cos BAC – T sin BAC =0.3 g and so T = 6.71N. Using radial acceleration gives T cos BAC + T sin BAC = 0.3ω2 x 0.6 sin BAC and so ω = 10.6. Answers: (i) ω = 5, 0.402J; (ii) T = 6.71, ω = 10.6
notes.key_messages:
• It is important for candidates to not spend too much time on any one question.
• It is important to read questions in detail and to be careful when copying expressions into answers.
• Candidates need to make full use of the supplied list of formulae.
notes.general_comments:
The work by most candidates was generally neat and well presented. Few candidates used premature
approximations and most candidates gave their answers to 3 significant figures. g = 9.8 or 9.81 was very
rarely seen. The paper clearly states that g = 10 should be used. Questions 1 and 3 proved to be the most
accessible questions on the paper. Questions 4 and 6 proved to be the most challenging.
